cards.q: Translate "The treaty fails unless the Senate consents." Which way does the arrow run, and what is the trap?
cards.a: If the Senate does NOT consent → the treaty fails. Contrapositive: the treaty doesn't fail → the Senate consented. Trap: the converse, "treaty fails → no consent" (it could fail for other reasons). Rule: "unless" = "if not", with the result on the then-side. Senate consent is necessary, not sufficient.
cards.history: ✘ Lesson #1; ✔ Lessons #2, #3.

cards.q: "Every country that has hosted the program for more than five years has seen an increase in favorable opinion. Country Z has seen no increase." What follows about Z? (Naming the rule is no longer tested, since Lesson #11; test the logic only.)
cards.a: Z has not hosted it for more than five years (five years or fewer, if at all). Contrapositive: "more than 5 yrs → increase" ≡ "no increase → not more than 5 yrs". Watch the boundary: "more than five" excludes exactly five.
cards.history: logic right every time; the name of the rule failed five times, so naming was dropped (Lesson #11).

cards.q: How do you test whether an answer choice is a necessary assumption? Apply it: "Four-day-week companies report higher job satisfaction, so a four-day week would raise satisfaction at Meridian." Why is "four-day-week employees work fewer total hours" not necessary?
cards.a: Negation test: negate the choice; if the argument then collapses, it is necessary. Necessary here: the higher satisfaction is not due entirely to other differences between the companies. Fewer hours is not necessary: negate it (same hours compressed into four days) and a four-day week could still raise satisfaction.

cards.q: On RC inference and main-point questions, why are "true-ish" or "the author would agree" answers often wrong, and which answer type usually wins?
cards.a: The answer must be licensed by the passage itself, not by what the author believes elsewhere. The most modest claim usually wins (not the "strongest"). Main-point trap: a detail promoted to main point. Extreme wording (every, all, no matter how) usually loses.
cards.history: ✔ Lessons #1–#3. PT 1: picked a "does not depend in any way" choice over a hedged one (see C032).

cards.q: Translate "The ceasefire will hold unless the border is closed." Which statement is valid: (i) "border closed → ceasefire fails" or (ii) "border NOT closed → ceasefire holds"? Give the contrapositive and a counterexample to the invalid one.
cards.a: Valid: (ii) ¬closed → holds. Contrapositive: ceasefire fails → border was closed (closure is necessary for failure). (i) is the inverse and is invalid: the border could close and the ceasefire hold anyway. Rule: "X unless Y" = "if not Y, then X".
cards.history: ✘ Lessons #2, #3; ✔ Lessons #4, #8. Right on fresh "unless" items since.

cards.q: A panel of 2 is chosen at random from 5 officers, 3 of whom are Political-cone. What is P(both Political)? Why is 0.6 × 0.6 = 36% wrong?
cards.a: 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 30%. Draws are without replacement, so the second pick is conditional: 2 of the remaining 4 are Political. 36% would be the answer only with replacement. Rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B given A).
cards.history: ✘ Lessons #2–#4; ✔3 Lessons #5, #6, #9.

cards.q: Which is correct, and why: "Walking into the embassy, the flag was visible above the gate" vs. "Walking into the embassy, she saw the flag above the gate"? Why doesn't passive voice rescue "Having walked into the embassy, the flag was seen by her…"?
cards.a: An opening participial phrase must describe the grammatical subject right after the comma. "She saw…" works; "the flag was…" makes the flag the walker (dangling modifier). The passive version still has "the flag" as its subject, so it still dangles. Test: ask "who or what is doing the -ing?"
cards.history: ✘ Lesson #2; ✔ Lessons #3, #5, #6.

cards.q: Country X makes 6 grain OR 6 cloth per day; Country Y makes 4 grain OR 2 cloth. Who has the comparative advantage in each good, and why can trade help both even though X is better at both?
cards.a: Opportunity costs: X: 1 cloth per grain, 1 grain per cloth. Y: 0.5 cloth per grain, 2 grain per cloth. Y has the comparative advantage in grain; X in cloth. Any trade price strictly between the two countries' opportunity costs leaves both better off. Compare opportunity costs, not raw output.
cards.history: ✔ Lessons #3, #5; ½ conf 3 in Lesson #13 (mechanism thin, no price range). Ask for a number next time.

cards.q: Translate "No attaché may enter the compound without clearance." Give the arrow, the contrapositive, and the trap.
cards.a: enter → clearance. Contrapositive: no clearance → cannot enter. Trap: the inverse "did not enter → no clearance". Rule: for "without", "requires", "only if", "no X without Y", the requirement is the necessary condition and goes on the THEN side; unlike "unless", there is no negation on the if-side. Shortcut: swap "No X without Y" for "Every X has Y", then write X → Y.

cards.q: "Every treaty the Senate ratifies was first approved by the Committee. No treaty the Committee approved is opposed by the Secretary of State. The Pacific accord is a treaty and the Secretary opposes it." What must be true, and why are "never submitted to the Committee" and "the Senate will never ratify it" wrong?
cards.a: Chain: ratified → committee-approved → not opposed by the Secretary. The Secretary opposes the accord, so it was not committee-approved, so it was not ratified. Answer: the Senate has not ratified it. "Never submitted" is a scope shift; "will never ratify" is too strong (future).
cards.history: ✔ Lessons #3, #4. Chains drilled again on Oct 19 (C046) and Nov 1 (the visa-officer item).

cards.q: What did McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) decide? Name the two holdings and the constitutional basis for each.
cards.a: (1) Congress may charter a national bank although the Constitution never mentions one: implied powers (Necessary and Proper Clause). (2) States may not tax a federal institution: the Supremacy Clause ("the power to tax is the power to destroy"). Chief Justice Marshall. Both favour federal power.
cards.history: ✘ Lesson #3; ½ Lessons #4–#6 (Supremacy Clause not named); ✔ Lesson #7.

cards.q: Country A makes 12 tractors OR 24 tons of grain per day; Country B makes 5 tractors OR 15 tons of grain. Who has the comparative advantage in tractors, and what trade price (grain per tractor) leaves both better off? What is the first step of the method?
cards.a: Step 1: write each opportunity cost as a number. A: 1 tractor = 2 grain. B: 1 tractor = 3 grain. A has the comparative advantage in tractors (B in grain). Any price between 2 and 3 grain per tractor leaves both better off.
cards.history: ✔ Lessons #4, #5, #6, #9. Habits: write the numbers, check the direction of the trade.

cards.q: Write each as an arrow and contrast them: (a) "The talks continue unless the delegation walks out." (b) "No ambassador may sign the accord without the Secretary's approval." Why does "unless" put a NOT on the if-side but "without" doesn't?
cards.a: (a) ¬walk out → talks continue (contrapositive: talks stop → walk out). (b) sign → approval (contrapositive: no approval → cannot sign). "X unless Y" = if not Y, then X. "A without B" = A requires B: A → B, with B on the THEN side. Shortcut for "without": "Every X has Y".
cards.history: ✘ Lessons #4, #6 (the converse); ½ Lesson #5; ✔ Lesson #7 (plain words: result and exception).

cards.q: A lawyer is faster than her assistant at both typing and legal work. Why should she still delegate the typing? Apply the same logic to a superpower and a smaller ally.
cards.a: Opportunity cost: every hour typing costs her valuable legal work; the assistant gives up far less by typing. Being better at both (absolute advantage) does not make trade pointless; gains from trade need only different opportunity costs. Ally version: the superpower's forces have a high opportunity cost, so letting an ally handle regional tasks is burden-sharing.
cards.history: ✔ Lessons #4, #5, #8. Ally half not yet asked.

cards.q: Socrates says "the unexamined life is not worth living." Write it as a conditional with its contrapositive. Does the unqualified wording prove that examination is the source of all value?
cards.a: Unexamined → not worth living; contrapositive: worth living → examined. Examination is a necessary condition (a gate or threshold). The text does not show it is sufficient or the only source of value; silence about other goods is not proof they have no value (compare "no one may practise surgery without a licence"). Answer from what the text licenses (C004).
cards.history: ✔2.8 Lesson #6.

cards.q: Describe the Socratic method in three steps, and say what the two kinds of counterexample show. Apply it to "Courage is staying at your post."
cards.a: (1) Get a definition. (2) Test it with a counterexample. (3) Accept that the definition fails, or refine it, and repeat until aporia (a productive dead end). A case that meets the definition but isn't the thing (enemy ran first; staying out of cowardice) shows the definition is not sufficient. A case that is the thing but fails the definition (leaving the post to rescue a friend) shows it is not necessary. A definition claims both directions.
cards.history: ½ Lessons #6–#8 (label swap); ✔ Lesson #11, whole card cold.

cards.q: "The talks continue unless the delegation walks out." Is the contrapositive safe with no extra assumption? Give it, and say what the converse would add.
cards.a: Contrapositive: talks stop → the delegation walked out. It follows from the arrow alone. The converse (talks continue → no walkout) is the trap: walking out is necessary for the talks to stop, not sufficient. Rule: the contrapositive is always safe; the converse and the inverse need extra assumptions.
cards.history: ✘ Lesson #6; ✔2.8 Lesson #7.

cards.q: Of 5 officers, 3 are Political-cone. Two are chosen at random without replacement. What is P(at least one is Political)? Before any numbers: what is the complement event in words?
cards.a: Complement of "at least one Political" = "neither is Political". Only 2 of the 5 are non-Political: 2/5 × 1/4 = 10%. So P(at least one) = 90%. Trap: 3/5 × 2/4 = 30% is "both Political", not "neither". Habit: name the event in words before any fractions.
cards.history: ✘ Lesson #6; ✔ Lesson #7; ✔3 Lesson #8.

cards.q: Given the arrow "no revocation → embassy stays open", write its converse, inverse and contrapositive. Which one is equivalent, and why are the other two traps?
cards.a: Converse (swap): embassy stays open → no revocation. Inverse (negate both in place): revocation → embassy doesn't stay open. Contrapositive (swap AND negate): embassy doesn't stay open → revocation. Only the contrapositive is equivalent; the others fail because the embassy could stay open even after a revocation.
cards.history: ✔3 Lesson #7; ½ Lesson #8; ✔ Lesson #12. Nov 1: his own wording of converse/inverse was muddled in a trap discussion; Nov 2: he named "converse" correctly for the ambassador choice (ii). Retest with arrows.

cards.q: Compute 4/6 × 3/5 with no calculator and no decimals. Why is converting 4/6 to 0.6 a trap?
cards.a: 4/6 = 2/3, and 2/3 × 3/5 = 6/15 = 2/5 = 40%. Cancel before multiplying. 4/6 is 0.667, not 0.6; rounding turned 40% into 36%. Rule: keep probabilities as fractions until the last step, write each step, sanity-check.
cards.history: ✘ Lesson #6; ✔ Lessons #7, #11.

cards.q: Take "If A, then B". Name the four moves and say which are valid: (1) A, so B. (2) not B, so not A. (3) B, so A. (4) not A, so not B.
cards.a: (1) Affirming the antecedent: valid. (2) Denying the consequent: valid (the contrapositive). (3) Affirming the consequent: invalid (converse). (4) Denying the antecedent: invalid (inverse). Both fallacies fail because A is sufficient for B but not necessary; they would be valid only for a biconditional.
cards.history: ✔ Lessons #7, #8. Names of the moves still unstable in use. PT 1: a parallel-flaw item that ran the arrow backward (C030).

cards.q: "A state receives the grant only if it passes the audit." Write the arrow. Does "only if" tell you that passing the audit is sufficient? How is "only if" different from "if and only if"? Give a quick test.
cards.a: grant → audit (requirement on the THEN side). "Only if" marks the audit as necessary, a gate; it does not make it sufficient. "If and only if" claims both directions. Test: can the result happen without X? If not, then result → X. Ticket picture: "You may board only if you have a ticket."
cards.history: ✘ Lesson #7; ✔2.8 Lesson #8; later slips in cold written arrows with "only" (C025, C033).

cards.q: "Every ally voted yes. Every committee member voted yes." What follows about allies and committee members? What is the chain rule, and what do you get from a chain's contrapositive?
cards.a: Nothing follows: both arrows END at "voted yes", and a shared end links nothing. Arrows link only when the END of one is the START of the next. The contrapositive runs backward through the whole chain. The converse of a chain is a trap.
cards.history: ✔3 Lesson #8. Reused in L16 (the river picture, C057).

cards.q: "Most analysts back plan A. Most analysts back plan B." (same group.) Must someone back both, and why? For 30 delegates, where most attended the morning session and most the afternoon, what is the smallest number who attended both? Show the arithmetic.
cards.a: Yes. "Most" = MORE than half, so the two groups together count more than the whole group, and the excess must be counted twice. Smallest "most" of N is the first whole number above N/2 (30 → 16). Minimum overlap = most + most − N: 16 + 16 − 30 = 2. Odd N → 1, even N → 2. Only works for the SAME group; "most + some" forces nothing.
cards.history: ✘ at conf 3 ×2 in Lessons #8–#9 (⚠️ cleared); ✔3 Lessons #10, #11, #12.

cards.q: "Of 30 delegates, most attended the morning session and most attended the afternoon session. A delegate is admitted to the closing dinner only if that delegate attended both sessions." Must at least two have attended both? Must at least two have been admitted? Why?
cards.a: Attended both: yes (16 + 16 − 30 = 2). Admitted: NOT forced. Arrow: admitted → attended both (a gate). "At least two admitted" runs the arrow backward (the converse). Habit: write the arrow first and ask which side the requirement goes on.
cards.history: ✘ at conf 3 Lesson #8 (⚠️ cleared); ✔ Lesson #9; ✔3 Lesson #11.

cards.q: Write the real logical opposite of each: (a) "All the delegates agreed." (b) "No delegate agreed." (c) "Some delegates agreed." (d) "Most delegates agreed." Why is "none agreed" not the opposite of "all agreed"?
cards.a: (a) Not all agreed (includes "none"). (b) Some agreed. (c) None agreed. (d) Half or fewer agreed. "All" and "none" can both be false, so they are not opposites. The opposite is the smallest change that breaks the claim.
cards.history: ✔ Lesson #9; ½ Lesson #11; ✔3 Lesson #12. Nov 1: "the opposite of 'fewer' is 'not fewer' (the same or more)" came up again (C056).

cards.q: Write the opposite of (a) "If the talks collapse, the aid is frozen." (b) "No cable is released without approval." Why is "If the talks collapse, the aid is NOT frozen" not the opposite of (a)?
cards.a: The opposite of "if A then B" is "A and not B". (a) The talks collapse AND the aid is not frozen. (b) A cable is released AND it was not approved. "If A then not B" can be true at the same time as the original, so it is not the opposite.
cards.history: ✘ Lesson #9; ✔3 faded; ½ Lesson #11; ✔3 Lesson #12. Extended to "or" and "and" in C044.

cards.q: How do you use the negation test on a necessary-assumption question, and why is an answer that merely restates a premise a trap? Apply it: "Every delegate who received the briefing packet voted for the resolution. So the packet persuaded delegates to vote for it." What kind of choice is necessary?
cards.a: Write the conclusion and the specific gap BEFORE any choice. Negate the choice correctly, then ask whether the CONCLUSION still follows. A restated premise adds nothing: its negation contradicts a premise, which is not the same as breaking the argument. Necessary here: some packet recipients would not have voted yes without the packet. Reject the converse, the restated premise, and the too-strong "the only thing that persuaded anyone". Link: C003, C046, C053, C057 (the sufficient-assumption mirror).
cards.history: ✘ at conf 3 in Lessons #9–#12 (four in a row); ✔ cold in Lessons #13 and #15 (⚠️ cleared; Box 2). Still thin on Oct 20: the first gap should be specific, and he missed the second gap (checked out vs. read). Nov 1 (not a scheduled test): gap-first and right on four fresh items (Varna, Dalton, consulate, tunnel) with the negation test applied correctly.

cards.q: On a necessary-assumption question, what do you write down BEFORE reading the choices? Apply it: "The ministry sold every armored car it owned last spring. None of the twelve cars it bought in 2020 appears in last spring's sales records. So none of those twelve cars was armored." What is the gap, and which three kinds of wrong answer do you reject?
cards.a: Before the choices: the conclusion in one line and the gap (the specific alternative that would break the argument). Here: an armored car from the 2020 batch could have left the fleet BEFORE last spring. Necessary: none of the twelve left the ministry before last spring. Reject: (a) restatements; (b) too-strong claims; (c) right topic that doesn't touch the gap. Check the pick with the negation test.
cards.history: seeded by PT 1 (5 of 9 non-timing misses in scored LR were in the assumption family). Original example. **Nov 2 (cold, conf 3): ✔** the conclusion ✔; the gap ✔ (a 2020 car sold before last spring); the assumption not stated as the negation of the gap, and the three kinds of wrong answer not asked. Box 2.

cards.q: On a sufficient-assumption ("the conclusion follows logically if…") or principle-justify question, what must the right answer do? Apply it: "If the aid budget is cut, most rural clinics will close. The aid budget has been cut. So most rural patients will lose access to care." Which choice justifies it: (i) "If most rural clinics close, most rural patients will lose access to care" or (ii) "If most rural clinics stay open, most rural patients will keep access to care"? Name the trap.
cards.a: The right answer bridges the gap: it starts from what the premises deliver and ends at the conclusion's new term. (i) does this. (ii) is the INVERSE of (i); it says what happens if the trigger does NOT occur, so it can't deliver the conclusion. A principle must mention the conclusion's terms and fire on the facts given.
cards.history: seeded by PT 1 (a justify item answered with the inverse). Original example. Links: C021, C022, C057, C058. L16 (Nov 2) taught the method; test this card cold.

log.note: Nov 4: bridge rule right, picked (i); did not name (ii) as the inverse trap

cards.q: "Critics say the new embassy compound is a waste of money. They are mistaken. The compound replaces three leased buildings, and within a decade the savings on rent will exceed its cost." What is the main conclusion, and what is the trap answer?
cards.a: Main conclusion: the critics are mistaken; the new compound is not a waste of money. "The rent savings will exceed the cost" is the support. Rule: when the author says "X is false" or "they are mistaken", that rebuttal IS the main conclusion. Test: "because" between the two candidates.
cards.history: PT 1: both rebuttal main points missed. ✔ Lesson #13 (first gave the support, then corrected; Box 2). Related: C049, C055.

cards.q: What is your LR pacing rule, and what are the five trap answer types you check every wrong choice against?
cards.a: Pacing: about 1:20 per question on average; at about 2:00 on any question, pick the best remaining answer, flag it and move on; come back only if time is left; never leave a blank. Traps: (1) too strong; (2) overreach from a hedge (the stimulus says can / need not, the choice says will / always); (3) half right; (4) restates a premise or the conclusion; (5) right topic, wrong logic (or the right logic in the wrong direction: converse/inverse).

Retest cold Tue.

cards.q: Athens says: "Justice is only talked about between equals in power." Write it as one arrow with the requirement on the THEN side. Is "If we are equals in power, then we may talk about justice" the same claim? What does the right arrow let you conclude about Melos?
cards.a: Talk of justice → equals in power. Equality is the necessary condition (a gate); it is not sufficient. "If equals, then we MAY talk about justice" is a permission and rules nothing out, so it is not the claim. Contrapositive: unequal → no justice talk. Melos is unequal to Athens, so (on Athens' premise) justice talk is out. Rule: "only", "only between", "without", "requires" put the requirement on the THEN side.
cards.history: ✘ Lesson #10; ✔ Lesson #12; ½ Lesson #13; ✔ Lesson #14 (cold). Precision: the claim is about talking about justice, not about justice itself.

cards.q: In the Melian Dialogue, what is Athens' position, and how does it answer each of the Melians' three appeals? Does Thucydides endorse it? Separate "should" from "will".
cards.a: Athens: the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must; justice is talked about only between equals (realism). The Melians appeal to (1) fair play as Athens' own long-term interest, (2) the gods, (3) Spartan help. Athens answers: (1) its subjects are watching, so sparing Melos would look like weakness (reputation); (2) gods and men both rule wherever they can; (3) hope is the comfort of the desperate (Sparta acts on its own interest, not on kinship). Melos refuses; no help comes; Athens kills the men and enslaves the rest. The speech describes how Athens argued; it is not Thucydides' own verdict (the Sicilian disaster follows, with no explicit link). Justice may deserve weight (should) without carrying weight in the outcome (will).
cards.history: ½ Lessons #12–#14; ✘ conf 0 Lesson #15 (Sparta pair); ✔ conf 3 Lesson #16 right after the 5-minute re-teach (not a cold retest). **Nov 2 (cold, unrated): ½.** Position ✔; Sparta ✔ (hope is the comfort of the desperate); gods ✔ in substance (worded "ruled by the same power-based logic"; Athens' claim is what gods and men DO); appeal 1 given as "justice" instead of fair play as Athens' own interest, and the reputation reply attached to Sparta. Image that worked: each appeal turns to something outside Athens' power (fairness, heaven, a friend) and Athens answers each with the same move: power and interest beat all three.

cards.q: An RC passage says an author narrates speech X, then event Y directly after it, draws no explicit connection, but "the placement is deliberate." Why is "X caused Y" a trap, and what is the supported inference?
cards.a: The passage licenses only a suggestion: the placement may invite the reader to see X's confidence as undercut by Y. "X caused Y" overreaches from a hedge (trap type 2, C032); so does "Y caused X": no cause in either direction is licensed. Other wrong answers: "the author endorses X" contradicts the passage; "readers are wrong to read the author at all" is too extreme. Name the specific flaw in each wrong answer. Picture (Nov 2): a film cuts from a man's boast to a storm; the cut never says the boast caused the storm, it makes you FEEL the boast is hollow. "Deliberate placement" works on the reader.

A mini-lesson with the film-cut picture followed. Missed-twice rule applied. Original item.

cards.q: A frost destroys half of this year's coffee crop. What happens to the price and to the quantity traded, and which curve shifts and which quantity moves along?
cards.a: Supply shifts left. Demand does not shift. The price rises, and buyers respond by buying less: the quantity demanded falls ALONG the unchanged demand curve (60 → 40 in the lesson table). Price up, quantity traded down. Rule: a non-price cause shifts the list of the side it hits; a price change moves you along the other side. Story: fewer sacks at market, buyers outbid each other, the price climbs until what buyers still want equals what sellers have.
cards.history: ½ conf 3 ⚠️ Lesson #12 (said demand shifted); ✔3 Lessons #13, #14 (⚠️ cleared).

cards.q: A fad adds buyers at every price while a frost cuts supply at the same time. What happens to the price, and what happens to the quantity traded? Is the equilibrium price an average of what buyers and sellers want?
cards.a: Demand shifts right and supply shifts left. Both push the price UP, so the price rises for certain. The two shifts push the quantity in opposite directions, so the quantity is uncertain: it depends on which shift is bigger. The equilibrium is not an average: it is the price at which the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer.
cards.history: ✔3 Lesson #14.

cards.q: "Fare-free weekends raised transit ridership by 30 percent, so fewer cars came downtown." Before any answer choice, state the gap in one line. What is the necessary assumption, and what happens when you negate it?
cards.a: Gap: the new riders may have been walkers or people who would not otherwise have travelled, so there is no proven switch from driving. Necessary assumption: at least some of the new riders would otherwise have driven downtown. Negation: none of the new riders would have driven, so the fall in cars is unexplained and the conclusion collapses. Link: C028, C053.
cards.history: ✔3 Lesson #11; ✘ Lesson #16 (restated the premise as the assumption; named the premise as the conclusion). **Nov 1 (cold, with C053, conf 2.7): ✔** the gap: new riders may be walkers or people who wouldn't have come downtown at all. Box 2.

cards.q: The staff-to-case ratio is 3 to 5, and there are 40 cases. How many staff? Then: 40 lawyers split between two offices in the ratio 3 to 5. How many in each? What do you do FIRST in both?
cards.a: Name the situation first. Staff and cases are DIFFERENT things: scale. 3/5 = x/40: 40 ÷ 5 = 8, 8 × 3 = 24 staff. The lawyers are PARTS OF ONE GROUP: add the parts (3 + 5 = 8), divide the whole (40 ÷ 8 = 5), multiply: 15 and 25. Different things: scale; parts of one group: add up to the whole. Fractions before decimals; write each step.
cards.history: ✔ Lesson #12 practice; ✔3 Lesson #14.

cards.q: 4 officers clear 18 cases in 3 days. How long do 6 officers take to clear 54 cases? And if the number of officers goes from 4 to 6, what is the percent change in officers, and in the days needed for the same job?
cards.a: Rate per officer-day: 18 ÷ (4 × 3) = 1.5 cases. 6 officers do 9 a day, so 54 ÷ 9 = 6 days. Percent: 4 → 6 officers is +50%, but the days for the same job fall from 3 to 2, which is −33⅓%. More workers means fewer days: an inverse relation, so the percent change differs (change ÷ the ORIGINAL number each time).
cards.history: ½ Lessons #12, #15, #16 (the days percent wrong three runs). **Nov 1 (cold, conf 2.7): ✔** 6 days, +50%, −33% with no nudge (the "from 3 to 2" step not written; keep asking). Box 2.

cards.q: Which branch holds the constitutional power to set tariffs, and how can a President impose them anyway? Give one reason Congress might regret delegating that power.
cards.a: Congress: Article I, Section 8 (duties and foreign commerce); it still holds it. A President acts only under authority Congress delegates by statute (e.g. the 2026 Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act: secondary tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, with a national-interest waiver). Congress can narrow or take back a delegation by a new law. Regret: one person can change trade policy quickly, or waive the very measure Congress mandated.
cards.history: ½ Lesson #13; ✔3 Lesson #15.

cards.q: Who imposed the 1973 oil embargo, against whom and why? What happened to the price, and in supply-and-demand terms what shifted?
cards.a: The Arab members of OPEC (OAPEC), led by Saudi Arabia, embargoed the US and some allies after the **Yom Kippur War of 1973** (Egypt and Syria attacked Israel; the US backed Israel) for backing Israel. Prices roughly quadrupled; long gas lines. Supply shifted left; demand did not shift, and buyers slid up along it. Short-run oil demand is inelastic, so the price jumped by more than the quantity fell (E4). A paucity of oil. The Six-Day War was 1967, six years earlier.

cards.q: If sanctions or tariffs remove a large share of a big supplier's oil from the market, what shifts, what slides along, and what happens to the price and the quantity traded? Why does the pump price jump, and why does that worry a government before an election?
cards.a: Supply shifts left; demand does not shift; buyers slide up along demand: price up, quantity traded down. Short-run oil demand is inelastic, so buyers cut back only a little and the price rises by more than the quantity falls. A government facing midterms fears it because voters feel prices directly. Credibility link: a threatened tariff works only if the executive follows through; a waived threat loses force (Athens' reputation argument in reverse, C034).
cards.history: ✔ Lesson #13 check; ✔3 Lesson #15 (said only "supply will shift"; say left).

cards.q: Write the real logical opposite of (a) "The delegation will bring a translator or a legal adviser." (b) "The embassy was closed and the staff was evacuated." Does plain "or" allow both parts to be true? State the swap rule.
cards.a: De Morgan: not (A or B) = not A AND not B; not (A and B) = not A OR not B. (a) No translator AND no legal adviser (neither): you must lock both doors to break an inclusive "or". (b) Not closed OR not evacuated (at least one part false breaks an "and"). Plain "or" is inclusive: both allowed, so the only world that breaks it is "neither". "Either… or… but not both" is the exclusive reading and must be stated. Same idea as the opposite of "all", "most" and "if A then B" (C026, C027): the smallest change that breaks the claim.
cards.history: pretest ✘ and check 2 of 3 (Lesson #14); ✔ Lesson #15 (fresh wording; skipped "does plain or allow both?" at first).

cards.q: What are the three steps of a GRE Text Completion item, and why does step 2 matter? Apply it: "A single forged signature can ______ an otherwise valid contract, stripping it of its legal force." (preclude / vitiate / obviate)
cards.a: (1) Read for the sentence's logic first: signal words (although, yet, but reverse; because, so, thus continue). (2) Write your OWN word for the blank before looking at the choices ("ruin", "invalidate"). (3) Match, then reread the whole sentence with the pick in it. Step 2 matters because a wrong-meaning word that sounds formal (like *preclude*) is rejected by your own prediction. Answer: *vitiate* (to spoil something so it loses force). *Preclude* rules out in advance (takes an event); *obviate* removes a need.

cards.q: "A grant is awarded only if the proposal passed both the technical review and the budget review. No proposal passes the budget review unless it was submitted before the deadline. Harbor's proposal was submitted after the deadline." Which must be true, and why is "Harbor would have received a grant had it been on time" wrong?
cards.a: Arrows: grant → (technical AND budget); budget review → on time. Chain: grant → budget review → on time. Contrapositive through the whole chain: late → no budget review → no grant. So Harbor did not receive a grant. "Would have received it if on time" mistakes a necessary condition for a sufficient one: the technical review and anything else could still fail. Wrong choices: a specific review result the stimulus never states; "every proposal that failed the budget review was late" is the converse of the second rule.

cards.q: A supply drop of 8% hits a market where buyers cut their quantity by 4% for every 10% price rise. By what percent must the price rise to clear the market? Does the price rise more or less than the quantity falls, and why? Name three things that make demand inelastic.
cards.a: Count steps: quantity to squeeze out ÷ squeeze per 10% price step: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 steps, so the price rises 20%. The price rises MORE than the quantity falls because buyers cut back little (demand is fairly inelastic). Rule: price rise = quantity to squeeze out ÷ squeeze per 10% × 10%. Sanity range: burgers (10% squeezed per step) → +10%; gasoline (1% per step) → +100%. Inelastic demand: a necessity, few substitutes, little time to adjust (short run). It is DEMAND that is inelastic, not the price. Picture: the price is a bouncer pushing buyers out the door, one step at a time. Links: C043, C042.
cards.history: ✘ then ✔ with the bouncer picture (Lesson #15); ✔ cold conf 2.8 Lesson #16 (still missing the reason the price rises more, and "little time to adjust" as the third cause). Box 2.

cards.q: Is the product of two consecutive integers always, sometimes or never even? Is 7,482 divisible by 3? By 9? Give the prime factorization of 84. If n² is odd, must n be odd?
cards.a: Always even: one of the two is even, and even × anything is even. 7+4+8+2 = 21: divisible by 3 (21 ÷ 3), not by 9. 84 = 2² × 3 × 7 (84 → 12 × 7 → 4 × 3 × 7 → 2 × 2 × 3 × 7). Yes, n² odd → n odd, by the contrapositive: n even → n² even. Rules: even × anything = even; odd × odd = odd; odd + odd = even; test 3 and 9 by digit sum, 4 by the last two digits, 5 by a last digit of 0 or 5; 1 is not prime, 2 is the only even prime.
cards.history: GQ1 check 3/3; ✔ with slips Lesson #16 (no digit-sum test; the exponent form of 84 not written, twice). Retest as the opening of GQ2 (Tue Nov 3).

cards.q: "Commentators claim that suspending the gasoline tax for the summer will lower pump prices. That claim is mistaken. Refiners cannot expand output within a single summer, and drivers will keep buying about as much whatever the price. So sellers can raise their own price by the amount of the tax cut, and the pump price will barely move. Besides, the suspension would cost the treasury billions." What is the main conclusion, and why is "Sellers will always raise their prices by the amount of any tax cut" wrong?
cards.a: Main conclusion: suspending the tax will not noticeably lower pump prices (the rebuttal "that claim is mistaken", with the hedge "barely"). Refiners, inelastic demand and sellers pocketing the cut are support; the treasury cost is an aside ("besides"). "Always" and "any tax cut" overreach from a hedge: the author says sellers CAN raise their price in this case (trap type 2, C032). Links: C031 (rebuttal main point), C043, C055, E5 (tax incidence).

cards.q: What is Glaucon's ring (of Gyges) argument in *Republic* II, and what does it claim about why people are just? What does he ask Socrates to prove?
cards.a: Give a just man and an unjust man a ring that makes them invisible, so neither can be caught or blamed: the just man would act exactly like the unjust one. So nobody is just willingly; people are just from fear of punishment or loss of reputation (justice as medicine for the person: put up with for its results). The challenge: show that justice is good in itself AND for its results, even for a man with the worst reputation and no reward (a SUFFICIENCY claim: justice alone is enough for a good life; L16 link). Links: Athens' premise in the Melian Dialogue (C034, C033). Glaucon's step is a contrapositive: if people valued justice for itself, the ring would not change their behavior.
cards.history: seeded by the Lesson #16 pretest (his consequentialist answer, then the one-purse point). **Nov 1 (cold, conf 2.6): ✔.** Justice as medicine ✔; "get away with it" ✔; the challenge ✔ in substance. Corrections: the medicine is for the person (avoid punishment, keep reputation), not for society; "even with the worst reputation" and "good in itself AND for results" not stated. Box 2.

cards.q: Name Glaucon's three kinds of goods and where he wants justice placed; then give Socrates' reply in one idea (the three parts of the soul) and say why the ring cannot touch it. What is the strongest objection (the psychopath)?
cards.a: Three kinds: (1) wanted for itself (joy); (2) wanted only for results (medicine); (3) both (health, knowledge). Glaucon wants justice in kind 3. Socrates: justice is the soul's health: reason rules, spirit (courage, honour) backs reason, appetite obeys; the unjust man is ruled by whichever desire shouts loudest (tyrannized from inside, unfree), so injustice is a disease even if never discovered. The ring protects against being caught, not against a diseased soul. Objection (his): a calm psychopath with no sense of justice looks like a counterexample, since the "sick" soul feels fine; Plato must stipulate what health is (the soul's structure, not its feelings).

cards.q: On the GRE Analyze an Issue task, what separates a 4 from a 6, and what should a thesis for "discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree" look like?
cards.a: A 4: a clear position, generic examples. A 6: a QUALIFIED position in one sentence ("X, because Y, except when Z"), specific named examples (events, policies, texts), the strongest counterargument answered, one pass of organization (thesis → reason 1 → reason 2 → counterargument → conclusion), and precise varied language. The instruction line changes the job: "extent" means a pure yes/no is a 4 at best. Test every example: does it support the point you use it for? (a reward is not a threat; checks and balances are not punishment.)

cards.q: In "Fare-free weekends raised transit ridership by 30 percent, so fewer cars came downtown", which clause is the conclusion, and where does the gap in a necessary-assumption item usually sit? Why is "the weekends caused the 30 percent rise" a trap?
cards.a: The conclusion follows "so" (fewer cars came downtown); the clause before it is the evidence (premise). The gap is the step from the evidence to the conclusion: the new riders might never have driven (walkers, new trips), so the necessary assumption is that at least some of them would otherwise have driven downtown. "The weekends caused the rise" restates the premise: negating it contradicts the premise and does not break the conclusion. Habit: underline the indicator ("so", "thus", "therefore", "hence"), write the conclusion, then ask what step connects the premise to it. Links: C028, C038.
cards.history: seeded by the C038 miss (premise named as the conclusion twice). **Nov 1 (cold, with C038, conf 2.7): ✔** the conclusion as the clause after "so" (he folded the cause "fare-free weekends caused…" into it) and the gap. Box 2.

cards.q: "Everyone agrees that a government should not spend money on projects whose benefits go mainly to people who are already wealthy. The proposed Harbor Tunnel would be paid for entirely out of public funds. Thus, the government should not build the Harbor Tunnel." What is the conclusion, what is the gap (a term shift), and what is the necessary assumption? Why is "the tunnel would be paid for entirely out of public funds" a trap?
cards.a: Conclusion: the government should not build the Harbor Tunnel (the clause after "Thus"). Gap: the rule is about who BENEFITS; the evidence is about who PAYS. Necessary assumption: the tunnel's benefits would go mainly to people who are already wealthy. Negation: the benefits would not go mainly to the wealthy, so the rule does not apply and the conclusion collapses. "Paid entirely out of public funds" restates the premise (trap type 4). Look for a term in the conclusion or the rule that the premises never mention.

log.note: conclusion (first said the assumption, self-corrected), assumption right; gap stated as a question, pays vs benefits term shift not named

cards.q: "Some analysts argue that raising the retirement age will inevitably hurt manual workers. But a higher retirement age could be paired with a partial early-pension option that protects them while still saving the pension fund money. So a higher retirement age need not hurt manual workers." What is the main conclusion, and why is "Raising the retirement age will not hurt manual workers" wrong?
cards.a: Main conclusion: a higher retirement age need not hurt manual workers (the rebuttal of the analysts, with the hedge "need not"). The early-pension option is the reason; "inevitably hurt" is the opposing view that the author answers. "Will not hurt" overreaches from the hedge "need not": the author says it can be avoided with the option, not that it will not happen (trap type 2, C032). Copy the conclusion clause with its hedge. Links: C031, C049.

cards.q: "Among first-year students who joined the mentoring program, 9 percent dropped out; among those who did not, 14 percent did. The dean concludes the program reduces first-year dropout." State the conclusion (with its direction), the gap, the necessary assumption, and what happens when you negate it. Which choice is the restated premise, and what does ITS negation do?
cards.a: Conclusion: the program reduces dropout. Gap: self-selection; the students who joined may have been less likely to drop out anyway (more conscientious). Necessary assumption: the joiners were not already less likely to drop out than the non-joiners. Negation: they were already less likely, so the gap between 9 and 14 is not the program's work and the conclusion collapses. Restated premise: "fewer joiners dropped out than non-joiners"; its negation ("not fewer": the same or more) contradicts the premise but does not touch the conclusion. The opposite of "fewer" is "not fewer", not just "more" (C026).

cards.q: What is a sufficient assumption, and how do you find it? Apply it: "Anyone who completes the safety course is assigned to the night shift. Priya has worked here for three years. Therefore, Priya will be assigned to the night shift." What must you add? Why does "too strong" stop being a flaw on these items?
cards.a: A sufficient assumption is ENOUGH: added to the premises, the conclusion MUST follow with no gap left. Method: write the conclusion; find the term the premises never connect (the course is never tied to three years); the answer is the arrow that joins them in the right direction. Chain: worked 3 years → completed the course → night shift; add "anyone who has worked over a year completes the course" (or "Priya completed the course"). River picture: the premises leave you on one bank, the rule is one stepping stone, the bridge is the missing stone (the chain rule, C023). A sweeping rule is fine if it delivers; the traps are the converse/inverse and answers that are only necessary. Links: C028 (necessary), C030, C058.
cards.history: seeded by the Lesson #18 pretest ✔ conf 3 (his own bridge: "anyone who has worked over a year completes the safety course"). Original item. His own words for the contrast: sufficient = the bridge to the other bank; necessary = the keystone that, if removed, breaks the argument.

cards.q: "Every report the ambassador signs goes to the Secretary. This cable is a report the ambassador drafted. So this cable will go to the Secretary." Which bridge works: (i) every report she drafts, she signs; (ii) every report she signs, she drafts; (iii) any report she does not sign does not go to the Secretary? Then: "no document negotiated on the public's behalf should stay secret unless publishing it would harm national security." Write the rule as an arrow and say which assumption makes "publish the agreement" follow.
cards.a: (i): it links the cable's term (drafted) to the rule's trigger (signed): drafted → signed → goes to the Secretary. (ii) is the converse (signing implies drafting; says nothing about drafting); (iii) is the inverse of the rule (speaks only about unsigned reports). Water agreement: secret → harm to national security; contrapositive: no harm → not secret. The sufficient assumption: publishing the agreement would not harm national security (it fires the contrapositive). The converse (if harm, keep it secret) can't deliver the conclusion.
cards.history: seeded by the Lesson #18 check ✔ (i, with the gap in his own words; (ii) named as the converse) and the water-agreement item ✔ A (conclusion and gap ✔; E explained as the wrong direction). Original items. Links: C030, C021, C033 ("unless"), C057.

cards.q: What is your method for a two-blank text completion item? Apply it: "Although the minister's critics dismissed his proposal as (i)____, even they conceded that its central analysis of the budget gap was (ii)____." (i) fatuous / trenchant / exigent; (ii) trenchant / spurious / perfidious. How can a fatuous proposal contain a trenchant analysis?
cards.a: Read the whole sentence and mark the signal words ("although… even they conceded" = contrast); start with the easier blank and predict your own word; do the other blank; the two blanks must make ONE sentence; a choice that fits one blank only is the trap. (i) fatuous (silly, pointless), (ii) trenchant (sharp, incisive). "Fatuous" is the CRITICS' verdict; the sentence turns on the concession: a sound diagnosis can come with a silly remedy. Always write the blank's word before looking at the choices (C045).

log.note: fatuous/trenchant right; own-word prediction not shown

cards.q: A town's grain sells 100 sacks at 10 coins. A ceiling of 6 cuts supply to 60 sacks while buyers want 140. Name the 80-sack gap, the 40 lost trades, and say what deadweight loss is.
cards.a: The 80-sack gap is a shortage (a paucity at the capped price): 140 wanted minus 60 supplied. It splits into 40 sacks that used to trade (100 to 60, the lost trades) plus 40 from new buyers the low price pulled in. Deadweight loss is the surplus (gains, in coins) from the lost trades: farmer and buyer would both have gained and no longer trade. A ceiling below equilibrium makes a shortage; a floor above it makes a surplus (a plethora).

cards.q: Who bears most of a tax, and does it matter who legally pays it? How does elasticity change the deadweight loss?
cards.a: The less elastic side (the one that cannot easily walk away) bears more of the tax; it does not matter who legally pays, since a tax on sellers and a tax on buyers split the cost the same way. If buyers are inelastic they keep buying, few trades vanish and the deadweight loss is small. If buyers can switch (rice), many trades vanish and the deadweight loss is large.

cards.q: Argument: 'Since bike lanes were painted on Harbor Street, shop sales fell 8%. Owners rightly blame the lanes. Removing them will restore sales.' What is the MAIN conclusion, and which necessary assumption states the gap in general form? Why is 'sales on other streets did not fall similarly' not necessary?
cards.a: Main conclusion: removing the lanes will restore sales (the lanes-caused-it claim is the intermediate step). General gap: the decline is not due to a cause that would remain in place after removal (a recession is one instance). Negate it: a persisting cause means removal won't restore, so the conclusion fails. 'Other streets did not fall' is a specific no-confounder answer: its negation (they fell similarly) does not break the argument, since the lanes could still be one cause. Prephrase the GENERAL gap, then pick the choice that states it; do not pick the answer matching your first guess.

cards.q: Aristotle, Politics: what two questions sort the six regimes, which are the sound and deviant forms of rule by one, few and many, and why is his 'democracy' a deviation?
cards.a: Questions: how many rule, and in whose interest (common advantage vs the rulers' own). One: kingship (sound) / tyranny. Few: aristocracy / oligarchy. Many: polity / democracy. Democracy is the poor majority ruling for itself, oligarchy the rich few ruling for themselves: both are class rule. Interest matters more than number. The most stable regime mixes the two and leans on a large middle class (the mean). Link: Athens at Melos ruled in its own interest (C034).

cards.q: Write the shape of a 6-level thesis in one sentence, and what must the 'except when' clause do? Test it on: 'Leaders should follow their own judgment rather than popular opinion.'
cards.a: [Claim], because [reason], except when [limit]; one sentence, 40 words or fewer, ONE position. The except-when must name a case where the OPPOSING view wins (e.g. leader's judgment unchecked or untrustworthy; a question that is the people's own to decide, like their rights or consent). It must not repeat or support the main claim (the nuclear-retaliation case does). Then test each example: does it support the point it is used for? (Mao's Cultural Revolution was leader-driven; Burke's Bristol speech fits the trustee view.)

cards.q: Write a GRE Issue thesis in one sentence of 40 words or fewer. What shape does it take, and what must the 'except when' do? (Nov 6 prompt: governments and future generations)
cards.a: Shape: claim, because reason, except when limit, in one breath, one position. The 'except when' must LIMIT the claim (a real exception), not support it. Model (38 words): Governments should put future generations' interests ahead of citizens' present wishes only when citizens consent, because the will of the unborn cannot be known, except when an irreversible existential threat looms that citizens ignore or do not understand. The sharp idea: who decides (through consent, not over it).

cards.q: A prompt says governments should put X AHEAD OF Y. Why is 'if governments did it always, no citizen would ever be served' a weak line of attack, and what is the better move? Also: how do you test each example?
cards.a: It refutes an extreme reading ('always') nobody asked about; the prompt only says 'ahead of' when they conflict. Answer the claim as stated, in its moderate form, and take a position on WHEN. Test every example: does it support the point you use it for? (Soviet utopia/Holodomor shows ideology plus dictatorship, not future-focus as such; global warming is a case for government action, so the 'except when' needs one line on why it does not swallow the rule.) Also keep the essay consistent: if future-focus is 'incompatible with democracy', do not later propose persuading citizens to act for their grandchildren.

cards.q: Why can't a democratic government easily act for future generations, and what is the sharpest way to state when it still may? (Consent and the unborn)
cards.a: Democratic legitimacy rests on the will of the living; the will of people not yet born cannot be known, so any claim to speak for them risks being a ruler's own agenda in disguise (the Soviet claim to a future utopia). So: act for the future THROUGH citizens' consent (persuade them: the world your grandchildren live in), not OVER it. Possible exception: an irreversible existential threat citizens ignore or do not understand. Links: Burke, Hobbes, Rousseau's general will, the Melian Dialogue (C034).
